source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Ksir_2016_CriticalOverviewPsychosis.pdf (Curr Psychiatry Rep 2016;18:12, version of record, published online 19 January 2016), pp. 1-11 (printed as Page N of 11), all text and the 70 references with annotations; full text extracted with pdftotext -layout, also page by page; Table 1 (p. 4) and p. 8 checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi; Table 2 read from the text layer.

claims.note: 'Shared vulnerability' is an accurate summary of Ksir & Hart's reading (abstract p. 1; conclusion p. 9). Their reading goes beyond their own evidence: the co-relative study they cite left a residual association after familial control, which they assign without data to non-inherited vulnerability (season of birth, infections, birth trauma; p. 8), and they conclude cannabis 'probably' does not in itself cause psychosis. The claim does not adopt that reading, and its 'none of these designs excludes a causal contribution' is the more defensible statement. Useful for the claim's description of the co-relative study: Ksir & Hart describe it as a Swedish national registry study in which most of the association disappeared after control for familial relationships (p. 8; ref. 39, whose title names it a Swedish national co-relative control study, p. 11); the viewpoint by Gillespie & Kendler does not say Swedish or registry. Ksir & Hart also cite the Australian polygenic-score study (Power et al., 2014) for schizophrenia liability predicting cannabis use, in line with the claim's reverse-direction point. Scope: 'recent research reports' (mostly 2013-2015) with no search method, structured by Hill's viewpoints.

anchors.extracted: Authors' reading: the evidence suggests cannabis does not in itself cause a psychotic disorder; early and heavy use are more likely in people with a vulnerability to psychosis and may be a prodromal sign; research focused only on the cannabis-psychosis association is of little value.

anchors.locator: Introduction, last paragraph; Literature Review, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Two hypotheses contrasted: cannabis as a contributing cause, and shared vulnerability (a diathesis raising the chances of both cannabis use and psychosis, which emerge at different ages, so early and heavy use precede diagnosis without causing it). The review covers recent research reports, organised by Hill's nine viewpoints; no search or selection method is given.

Swedish national registry study (ref. 39, Giordano et al.): clear association between cannabis use and schizophrenia, most of which disappeared after control for familial relationships; any residual non-familial link attributed by the authors to non-inherited vulnerability. Australian twin study (ref. 59): higher polygenic risk for schizophrenia associated with more cannabis use. US family study (ref. 60): morbid risk of schizophrenia raised in families of people with psychosis whether or not they used cannabis. The authors call these strong evidence for shared vulnerability over a contributing cause; no effect sizes given.

Cannabis use preceding psychosis and a gradient with heavier use are both read as consistent with either hypothesis, because heavier naturally occurring use also carries more associated risk factors (early and heavy tobacco and alcohol use) and can mimic a dose-response without a direct effect.

Studies built on the assumption that cannabis might raise psychosis risk have produced neither a mechanism nor an effective way to reduce risk by reducing use, which the authors attribute to cannabis probably not causing such an increase; early and heavy use are more likely in people vulnerable to a range of problem behaviours, and in some the same vulnerability raises the risk of psychosis or another mental disorder.

claims.note: Matches p. 8: at least a tenfold rise in UK cannabis use since the 1970s, attributed to Gage et al. [2] (ref. 2: Gage, Zammit & Hickman, 2013, F1000 Medicine Reports, the 'commentary'); first admissions for schizophrenia show no increase, perhaps a slight decrease; Ksir & Hart present this as a semi-experimental test that goes against the causal hypothesis. Two small points: (1) in Ksir & Hart only the tenfold rise carries the citation; the first-admissions statement has none, so 'according to a commentary' for both halves is an inference (probably correct, but the admissions data cannot be traced from this source); (2) the same paragraph gives a second UK item the claim leaves out: hospital admissions for cannabis psychosis fell after the 2004 relaxation of cannabis classification and rose after the 2009 return, opposite to prediction (ref. 64, Hamilton et al., 2014), though the authors doubt use changed much. That item concerns acute cannabis-psychosis admissions and legal status, not schizophrenia incidence as use rose, so leaving it out is defensible. The claim's 'ecological' label is apt; Ksir & Hart's 'semi-experimental' is their own framing.

anchors.extracted: Citing Gage et al. [2], UK cannabis use rose at least tenfold since the 1970s; the authors state that first admissions for schizophrenia showed no increase, perhaps a slight decrease, over that time (no citation for the admissions data), contrary to what a causal effect would predict. Also: after the 2004 relaxation and the 2009 tightening of cannabis classification, hospital admissions for cannabis psychosis fell and then rose, opposite to prediction (ref. 64), though the changes probably had little effect on use.

Ref. 2 is Gage, Zammit & Hickman (2013), F1000 Medicine Reports 5, 'Stronger evidence is needed before accepting that cannabis plays an important role in the aetiology of schizophrenia in the population': the commentary behind the tenfold figure.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high (search, separation of evidence from speculation, balance). No reference has Ksir or Hart as author, so 'low' for reliance on own studies is right.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. The card's point (6) holds: monozygotic co-twins share season of birth, so it cannot explain a residual within-pair association. Also, the review presents an uncontrolled national time trend as a 'semi-experimental' test (p. 8).
